subModules.title: Reading Mission: Building a Clear Academic Argument

content.summary: Read a short article about how students can organise an academic essay. You will identify a thesis statement, trace how topic sentences support its argument, and notice how nominalisation and transition signals make ideas more connected and formal.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Recognise thesis statements built from a topic, a controlling idea, and a clear scope. Identify topic sentences that connect paragraph points to the thesis, as well as nominalised forms such as improve and improvement.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Learn words for academic argument and organisation, including thesis statement, topic sentence, controlling idea, nominalisation, cohesion, and transition signal.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the introduction and topic sentences to find the main argument. Then scan for transition signals, nominalised words, and details that explain how each paragraph supports the thesis.

learningObjectives: Identify the main claim and scope of a short academic text.
Locate topic sentences and explain how they support the thesis.
Recognise nominalised forms and describe their effect on academic style.
Use transition signals to follow relationships between ideas.

contextWarmup.prompt: You are planning an essay about public transport. Which opening claim gives readers the clearest guide to the argument?
options: Improving public transport can reduce urban traffic because it offers commuters a reliable alternative to driving.
Public transport is an interesting subject that many people discuss.
This essay is about buses, trains, and cities.
contextWarmup.explanation: This option names the topic, makes a clear claim, and gives a reason that can guide the essay. The other options introduce the subject but do not state a focused argument.

rules: A thesis statement usually names the topic, presents the writer's controlling idea, and indicates the reasons or scope of the essay.
A topic sentence introduces one main point in a body paragraph and should connect that point to the thesis.
Nominalisation changes a verb or adjective into a noun, as in develop to development or significant to significance. It can make academic writing more concise and formal.
Transition signals such as furthermore, in contrast, and as a result show how one idea relates to another.

commonTrap.explanation: A broad topic is not the same as a thesis. A thesis needs a specific claim, and each body paragraph needs a clear point that supports it.
commonTrap.wrong: This essay is about remote work.
commonTrap.correct: Remote work can improve employee productivity by reducing commuting time and allowing more flexible schedules.

content.passageTitle: From a Broad Topic to a Clear Argument
paragraphs: When students begin an academic essay, they sometimes choose a topic but do not yet have an argument. A thesis statement does more than announce a subject: it makes a focused, arguable claim and sets a useful scope. For example, an essay about remote work could argue that it improves employee well-being by reducing commuting time and giving workers more control over their schedules. This claim tells readers both what the essay is about and what it will show.

Each body paragraph then develops one part of that argument. A topic sentence names the paragraph's main point and links it to the thesis. First, remote work can reduce the stress caused by daily travel. The rest of the paragraph should explain this point with evidence, examples, or reasoning. A paragraph about flexible schedules could support a different part of the same thesis. If a paragraph introduces an unrelated point, the writer may need to revise the thesis or remove that paragraph.

Cohesion helps readers see how the parts fit together. Transition signals such as furthermore can introduce an additional reason, while however can show a contrast. Writers can also repeat key terms or use clear pronouns to connect sentences. These choices should guide the reader rather than decorate the text. A transition signal cannot fix a weak argument, so the logical relationship between two ideas must be clear before a connector is added.

Nominalisation can give academic writing a more formal and compact style. For example, writers can change improve to improvement: The new schedule improved staff well-being becomes The improvement in staff well-being followed the introduction of the new schedule. The second version focuses on the result, but it may sound less direct. Writers should choose a nominalised form when it helps the sentence, not simply to make the language seem more academic. Clear claims, focused topic sentences, and meaningful connections remain the most important parts of an effective essay.

pairs.right: A focused claim that guides an essay
A sentence that introduces a paragraph's main point
Changing a verb or adjective into a noun
Logical connections between parts of a text

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a thesis statement, according to the passage?
options: To make a focused claim and set the scope of the essay
To list every source the writer plans to use
To introduce an unrelated example
questions.answer: To make a focused claim and set the scope of the essay
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says that a thesis statement makes an arguable claim and sets a useful scope.

questions.question: Which claim does the example essay make about remote work?
options: It improves employee well-being by reducing commuting time and increasing control over schedules.
It prevents employees from working with other people.
It makes every organisation more flexible.
questions.answer: It improves employee well-being by reducing commuting time and increasing control over schedules.
questions.explanation: The passage gives this as the example thesis claim about remote work.

questions.question: What should a topic sentence do?
options: Name the paragraph's main point and link it to the thesis
Introduce a new subject that is unrelated to the essay
Repeat the full thesis without adding a paragraph point
questions.answer: Name the paragraph's main point and link it to the thesis
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that a topic sentence identifies the main point and connects it to the thesis.

questions.question: What does the passage recommend for the rest of a body paragraph after its topic sentence?
options: Explain the point with evidence, examples, or reasoning
Add several transition signals without explanation
Introduce a completely different argument
questions.answer: Explain the point with evidence, examples, or reasoning
questions.explanation: The passage says that the rest of the paragraph should explain the topic sentence's point using evidence, examples, or reasoning.

questions.question: What might a writer do if a paragraph introduces an unrelated point?
options: Revise the thesis or remove the paragraph
Add more nominalisations to the paragraph
Keep it and add the word furthermore
questions.answer: Revise the thesis or remove the paragraph
questions.explanation: The passage says an unrelated paragraph may mean the writer needs to revise the thesis or remove that paragraph.

questions.question: What relationship can furthermore signal?
options: An additional reason
A contrast
A conclusion that rejects the earlier point
questions.explanation: The passage explains that furthermore can introduce an additional reason.

questions.question: Why should writers check the logical relationship between ideas before adding a transition signal?
options: A transition signal cannot repair a weak argument.
Transition signals are not allowed in academic writing.
A connector always changes the meaning of a claim.
questions.answer: A transition signal cannot repair a weak argument.
questions.explanation: The passage states that the logical relationship must be clear because a transition signal cannot fix a weak argument.

questions.question: Which word is the nominalised form of improve in the example?
options: improvement
improved
improving
questions.explanation: The passage directly identifies improvement as the noun form of improve.

questions.question: What is one possible disadvantage of the sentence using nominalisation?
options: It may sound less direct.
It cannot describe a result.
It always makes the claim informal.
questions.explanation: The passage says the nominalised version focuses on the result but may sound less direct.

questions.question: What does the passage say writers should consider when using nominalisation?
options: Use it when it helps the sentence, not just to sound more academic.
Use it in every sentence of a formal essay.
Replace every verb with a noun.
questions.answer: Use it when it helps the sentence, not just to sound more academic.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph advises writers to choose a nominalised form when it helps the sentence rather than using it only to appear academic.

keyPhrases.note: Common casual request used among students seeking feedback on an essay.
Refers to a thesis statement that takes a stance rather than stating a known fact.
A phrasal verb meaning to reduce options or make a topic more specific.
Refers to clear cohesion and smooth transitions linking paragraphs together.

connectedSpeech.slow: Could you look at my thesis?
connectedSpeech.note: The modal 'could' fuses with 'you' to form /kədʒə/, and the final /k/ in 'look' links directly into 'at'.

connectedSpeech.slow: That sounds like a broad fact.
connectedSpeech.note: The /d/ in 'sounds' is frequently elided before the consonant /l/, blending smoothly into 'like a'.

connectedSpeech.slow: What about the first topic sentence?
connectedSpeech.note: The final /t/ in 'what' becomes a fast flap tap, and the /t/ in 'first' drops before 'topic'.

connectedSpeech.slow: Always keep the logical chain clear.
connectedSpeech.note: The unreleased bilabial stop /p/ transitions directly into the dental fricative without a break.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Structuring Academic Theses and Topic Sentences

content.summary: This guide demonstrates how to construct clear thesis statements, focused topic sentences, and formal academic prose using nominalisation and precise transitions.

blueprintItems.title: The Academic Thesis Statement Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Topic + Controlling Idea + Sub-arguments or Scope
blueprintItems.example: The expansion of renewable energy sources reduces fossil fuel dependence, stimulates local job growth, and lowers carbon emissions.

blueprintItems.title: The Paragraph Topic Sentence Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Transition Signal + Specific Sub-topic + Controlling Idea linked to Thesis
blueprintItems.example: Primarily, the development of solar infrastructure creates sustainable employment opportunities in regional communities.

blueprintItems.title: Academic Nominalisation Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Verbal/Adjectival Clause -> Abstract Noun Phrase + Formal Predicate
blueprintItems.example: Because cities are growing rapidly, public transit demands are rising -> The rapid expansion of cities increases demand for public transport.

mechanicsRules.rule: Avoid conversational first-person announcements in thesis statements.
mechanicsRules.badExample: In this essay I will discuss why plastic bags should be banned.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: A nationwide prohibition of single-use plastics reduces marine pollution and encourages sustainable retail habits.
mechanicsRules.why: Academic writing requires an objective focus on the topic rather than self-referential statements about the author.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place a comma after introductory transitional phrases at the start of topic sentences.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Furthermore urban green spaces improve resident mental health.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Furthermore, urban green spaces improve resident mental health.
mechanicsRules.why: Introductory transitional adverbials require a following comma to separate them from the main clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Maintain parallel grammatical structure when listing points in a thesis statement.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The scheme improves literacy, reducing crime rates, and creates economic stability.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The scheme improves literacy, reduces crime rates, and creates economic stability.
mechanicsRules.why: Parallel series of actions must use matching grammatical verb forms to ensure syntactic balance.

sampleSentences.en: The implementation of automated traffic systems significantly decreases urban congestion during peak hours.
sampleSentences.id: Penerapan sistem lalu lintas otomatis secara signifikan mengurangi kemacetan perkotaan pada jam sibuk.
sampleSentences.focus: Nominalisation of 'implement' to 'implementation' for formal register

sampleSentences.en: Consequently, public investment in vocational education strengthens workforce resilience against technological disruption.
sampleSentences.id: Oleh karena itu, investasi publik pada pendidikan vokasi memperkuat ketahanan tenaga kerja terhadap disrupsi teknologi.
sampleSentences.focus: Introductory transition paired with clear topic and controlling idea

sampleSentences.en: Although online learning offers geographic flexibility, it diminishes interpersonal collaboration among university students.
sampleSentences.id: Meskipun pembelajaran daring menawarkan fleksibilitas geografis, hal tersebut mengurangi kolaborasi antarpribadi di kalangan mahasiswa.
sampleSentences.focus: Complex sentence thesis with a counter-argument concession

sampleSentences.en: The destruction of coastal wetlands compromises regional flood defences and destabilises local ecosystems.
sampleSentences.id: Kerusakan lahan basah pesisir membahayakan pertahanan banjir daerah dan mengacaukan ekosistem lokal.
sampleSentences.focus: Nominalised subject followed by parallel verbs

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Add a comma after the transition, punctuate items in a list, and maintain parallel past participles.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Draft an Objective Thesis Statement
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write an academic thesis statement on whether universities should make all course materials digital. State your clear position and list two supporting arguments using parallel structure. Do not use first-person pronouns like 'I think' or 'In my opinion'.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Replacing printed textbooks with digital course materials reduces educational expenses for students and enhances access to updated research.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Draft a Cohesive Topic Sentence
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a formal topic sentence for a body paragraph supporting the view that remote work benefits employers. Include a transition signal, mention the specific focus (such as operational costs), and use nominalisation.
guidedLabChallenges.example: In addition, the adoption of remote work practices significantly reduces corporate expenditure on office maintenance and utilities.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite this subjective statement into an objective academic thesis statement by removing first-person language:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I believe that governments should subsidise solar energy because it cuts pollution.
practicumQuestions.hint: Begin directly with 'Governments should subsidise solar energy because...'
targetAnswers: Governments should subsidise solar energy because it cuts pollution.
Governments should subsidise solar energy because it reduces pollution.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Academic statements remove subjective phrases like 'I believe that' to maintain an objective tone.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the clause using the noun form of the underlined verb: 'When the committee decided, public debate ended.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: When the committee decided, public debate ended. -> The committee's ________ ended public debate.
targetAnswers: The committee's decision ended public debate.
decision
practicumQuestions.explanation: The noun form of 'decide' is 'decision', which makes the sentence more concise and formal.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the punctuation and capitalisation in this topic sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: moreover public libraries provide essential digital access for disadvantaged citizens
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalise the transition and insert a comma immediately after it.
targetAnswers: Moreover, public libraries provide essential digital access for disadvantaged citizens.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Transitional adverbs at the start of a sentence require an initial capital letter and a following comma.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences using 'whereas' to highlight the contrast in an academic style:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Traditional classrooms require fixed schedules. Online courses offer scheduling flexibility.
practicumQuestions.hint: Join both clauses into one sentence with 'whereas' preceded by a comma.
targetAnswers: Traditional classrooms require fixed schedules, whereas online courses offer scheduling flexibility.
Whereas traditional classrooms require fixed schedules, online courses offer scheduling flexibility.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Whereas' expresses an academic contrast between two parallel clauses.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the non-parallel verb in this thesis statement:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Stricter vehicle emissions standards protect public health, lower greenhouse emissions, and creating cleaner urban spaces.
targetAnswers: Stricter vehicle emissions standards protect public health, lower greenhouse emissions, and create cleaner urban spaces.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Elements in a coordinate series must share identical verb tense and form ('protect', 'lower', 'create').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Convert the informal cause-and-effect sentence into a nominalised subject: 'Because global temperatures are rising, sea levels continue to climb.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: The ________ of global temperatures causes sea levels to continue to climb.
practicumQuestions.hint: Supply the noun form of the verb 'rise'.
targetAnswers: rise
rising
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'The rise of global temperatures' packages the verbal action into an abstract noun phrase.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the topic sentence by adding the most fitting formal transition signal of contrast:
practicumQuestions.promptText: ________, despite substantial investments in automated public transit, commuter delays remain frequent.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use a formal transition such as 'However' or 'Nevertheless'.
targetAnswers: However
Nevertheless
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'However' and 'Nevertheless' signal that the sentence contrasts with earlier positive arguments.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Identify and correct the comma splice in this academic thesis statement:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Electric vehicles decrease urban air pollution, they increase the demand for electrical grid capacity.
practicumQuestions.hint: Add 'but' or 'yet' after the comma, or use 'although' at the beginning.
targetAnswers: Electric vehicles decrease urban air pollution, but they increase the demand for electrical grid capacity.
Electric vehicles decrease urban air pollution, yet they increase the demand for electrical grid capacity.
Although electric vehicles decrease urban air pollution, they increase the demand for electrical grid capacity.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Two independent clauses cannot be joined solely by a comma; a coordinating conjunction like 'but' or a subordinator like 'although' is required.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite this announcement phrase into an argumentative thesis: 'This paper will examine the benefits of bilingual education for cognitive agility.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: Begin your sentence directly with 'Bilingual education improves...'
practicumQuestions.hint: State the direct effect without saying what the paper will do.
targetAnswers: Bilingual education improves cognitive agility and enhances long-term linguistic competence.
Bilingual education improves cognitive agility in young learners.
Bilingual education improves cognitive agility.
practicumQuestions.explanation: An argumentative thesis directly asserts a claim rather than announcing the paper's contents.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Formulate a single topic sentence that introduces the environmental benefits of reforestation:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Include a transition signal, the topic (reforestation), and the controlling idea (environmental restoration).
practicumQuestions.hint: You may start with 'First and foremost,' or 'In the first place,'.
targetAnswers: First and foremost, large-scale reforestation contributes significantly to the restoration of degraded ecosystems.
First and foremost, reforestation plays a vital role in environmental restoration and carbon capture.
In the first place, large-scale reforestation contributes significantly to regional environmental restoration.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A complete topic sentence contains an introductory transition, defines the sub-topic, and indicates the paragraph's specific controlling idea.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Building Clear Academic Arguments

content.summary: Practise explaining how a thesis statement guides an essay and how topic sentences support its controlling idea. Speak in complete sentences, use formal transitions, and make nominalised forms such as development and analysis clear.
content.audioGuidance: Give key academic terms enough time to be understood. Stress the main content words, link familiar words naturally, and pause briefly between the claim and its supporting reasons. Use falling intonation for completed claims and a slight rise when checking or inviting agreement.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear vowel sounds in academic vocabulary
pillars.explanation: Keep the vowel sounds distinct in words such as thesis, reason, and cohesion. Avoid rushing the middle syllables of longer words.

pillars.name: Word Stress
pillars.explanation: Place the strongest beat on the correct syllable in words such as cohesion, nominalisation, and analysis. Practise each word slowly before using it in a sentence.

pillars.name: Academic Rhythm
pillars.target: Clear sentence stress and controlled pauses
pillars.explanation: Emphasise the claim and its reasons, while keeping articles and prepositions lighter. Pause briefly before a transition signal when it introduces a new point.

pillars.name: Intonation
pillars.target: Falling intonation for claims and rising intonation for checks
pillars.explanation: Let your voice fall at the end of a complete argument. Use a gentle rise when asking whether a thesis or topic sentence is clear.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The main stress falls on the first syllable in thesis and the second syllable in statement.
Topic is stressed on its first syllable, while sentence is stressed on its second.
Both words have three syllables, with the main stress on the middle syllable.
Nominalisation has its main stress near the end, while controlling is stressed on its second syllable.

drills.targetText: A strong thesis statement presents a clear, arguable claim.
drills.phonetic: /ə strɒŋ ˈθiːsɪs ˈsteɪtmənt prɪˈzents ə klɪə ˈɑːɡjəbəl kleɪm/
drills.focus: Word stress in thesis statement and clear delivery of the main claim
drills.hint: Stress thesis, statement, clear, and claim. Pause briefly before the final phrase.

drills.targetText: Each topic sentence supports the controlling idea of the essay.
drills.phonetic: /iːtʃ ˈtɒpɪk ˈsentəns səˈpɔːts ðə kənˈtrəʊlɪŋ aɪˈdɪə əv ði ˈeseɪ/
drills.focus: Sentence stress and clear articulation of topic sentence
drills.hint: Make topic sentence and controlling idea easy to hear, then let your voice fall at the end.

drills.targetText: The development of public transport can reduce urban traffic.
drills.phonetic: /ðə dɪˈveləpmənt əv ˈpʌblɪk ˈtrænspɔːt kən rɪˈdjuːs ˈɜːbən ˈtræfɪk/
drills.focus: Nominalisation and natural rhythm in a formal academic sentence
drills.hint: Say development as one clear word and give reduce a strong beat.

drills.targetText: Furthermore, this evidence strengthens the argument and improves cohesion.
drills.phonetic: /ˌfɜːðəˈmɔː ðɪs ˈevɪdəns ˈstreŋθənz ði ˈɑːɡjumənt ənd ɪmˈpruːvz kəʊˈhiːʒən/
drills.focus: Transition signal, connected speech, and cohesion stress
drills.hint: Pause after Furthermore. Keep the sentence moving, then stress cohesion clearly.

roleplay.context: You are meeting your academic writing tutor to discuss an essay about whether universities should make public transport more affordable for students. You need to present a thesis and explain how your topic sentences will support it.

turns.speaker: Academic Writing Tutor
turns.text: What is the main claim you want your essay to make?
turns.translation: Apa klaim utama yang ingin kamu sampaikan dalam esaimu?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: My thesis is that universities should subsidise public transport because it reduces students' travel costs and car use.
turns.translation: Tesis saya adalah bahwa universitas sebaiknya memberi subsidi transportasi umum karena hal itu mengurangi biaya perjalanan dan penggunaan mobil oleh mahasiswa.

turns.speaker: Academic Writing Tutor
turns.text: How will your first topic sentence support that thesis?
turns.translation: Bagaimana kalimat topik pertamamu akan mendukung tesis tersebut?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: It will focus on the reduction of travel costs, and the next paragraph will explain the environmental benefit.
turns.translation: Kalimat itu akan berfokus pada pengurangan biaya perjalanan, dan paragraf berikutnya akan menjelaskan manfaat bagi lingkungan.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds about how you would plan an academic essay, using the three points as a guide.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe how you would move from an essay topic to a clear thesis and supporting paragraphs.
storyPoints: Choose an essay topic and decide what specific issue you will address
State an arguable thesis with a clear controlling idea
Plan topic sentences that support the thesis in a logical order
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My thesis makes a clear claim, and each topic sentence supports one part of that argument.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ ˈθiːsɪs meɪks ə klɪə kleɪm ənd iːtʃ ˈtɒpɪk ˈsentəns səˈpɔːts wʌn pɑːt əv ðæt ˈɑːɡjumənt/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Organise your explanation in a clear sequence and show how the essay's parts support one central claim.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds about how you would improve the cohesion of a short academic essay.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell a short story about revising a draft so its thesis, topic sentences, and transitions work together.
storyPoints: Identify a paragraph that does not clearly support the thesis
Revise its topic sentence to make the controlling idea more specific
Add a suitable transition signal and explain how the revision improves cohesion
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I revised the topic sentence and added a transition signal, so the argument became easier to follow.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ rɪˈvaɪzd ðə ˈtɒpɪk ˈsentəns ənd ˈædɪd ə trænˈzɪʃən ˈsɪɡnəl səʊ ði ˈɑːɡjumənt bɪˈkeɪm ˈiːziə tə ˈfɒləʊ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past-tense verbs to describe revision and explain the logical effect of each change.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond to the tutor and state a clear, arguable thesis for the essay topic.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your tutor asks you to present your position on whether universities should require students to attend lectures.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: In a live tutorial, you are discussing an essay about compulsory lecture attendance. Explain your position in one focused thesis statement.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student presenting an academic argument. The tutor expects a specific claim rather than a general statement about the topic.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Universities should not require attendance at every lecture because flexible access can support different learning needs.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˌjuːnɪˈvɜːsɪtiz ʃʊd nɒt rɪˈkwaɪə əˈtendəns æt ˈevri ˈlektʃə bɪˈkɒz ˈfleksəbəl ˈækses kən səˈpɔːt ˈdɪfrənt ˈlɜːnɪŋ niːdz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Make your position explicit and give a reason that narrows the scope of the argument.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Give the tutor a topic sentence that supports a thesis about affordable student housing.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your tutor asks how your first body paragraph will support your claim that affordable housing helps students succeed.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are planning a body paragraph for an essay arguing that universities should help students find affordable housing.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student explaining the role of a topic sentence. Connect one specific reason to the essay's thesis.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Affordable housing reduces financial pressure, allowing students to devote more time to their studies.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /əˈfɔːdəbəl ˈhaʊzɪŋ rɪˈdjuːsɪz faɪˈnænʃəl ˈpreʃə əˈlaʊɪŋ ˈstjuːdənts tə dɪˈvəʊt mɔː taɪm tə ðeə ˈstʌdiz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Keep the topic sentence focused on one supporting reason and make its connection to the thesis clear.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond by using a nominalised form to make the point sound concise and formal.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your tutor asks you to rewrite the idea 'cities should develop more cycle routes' in a formal academic style.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: During a writing consultation, you are revising an informal sentence about cycle routes into a concise academic point.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student practising nominalisation. Explain the idea using development or another suitable noun form.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The development of additional cycle routes could reduce traffic in city centres.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə dɪˈveləpmənt əv əˈdɪʃənəl ˈsaɪkəl ruːts kʊd rɪˈdjuːs ˈtræfɪk ɪn ˈsɪti ˈsentəz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a noun form such as development to express the action in a more formal structure.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose a transition signal that shows contrast, then explain how it connects the ideas.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your tutor says one study supports online learning, while another reports that some students feel isolated. How would you connect these points?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are discussing evidence with a tutor and need to show a contrast between the benefits and limits of online learning.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student selecting a formal transition signal and making the relationship between two ideas clear.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: In contrast, some students report feeling isolated during online courses.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪn ˈkɒntrɑːst sʌm ˈstjuːdənts rɪˈpɔːt ˈfiːlɪŋ ˈaɪsəleɪtɪd ˈdjʊərɪŋ ˈɒnlaɪn ˈkɔːsɪz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a transition signal that accurately shows the logical relationship between the two points.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Explain the meaning of controlling idea, then use it in a sentence about an essay.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: What does controlling idea mean, and how can it make a topic sentence more focused?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The controlling idea limits the topic and shows what the paragraph will explain.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə kənˈtrəʊlɪŋ aɪˈdɪə ˈlɪmɪts ðə ˈtɒpɪk ənd ʃəʊz wɒt ðə ˈpærəɡrɑːf wɪl ɪkˈspleɪn/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Define the term in your own words and use it accurately in a sentence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Turn the verb phrase develop public transport into a sentence using the nominalisation development.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Rewrite this idea formally: 'The city should develop public transport to reduce car use.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The development of public transport could reduce car use.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə dɪˈveləpmənt əv ˈpʌblɪk ˈtrænspɔːt kʊd rɪˈdjuːs kɑː juːs/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use development as a noun and keep the relationship between the action and its result clear.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say nominalisation clearly, placing the strongest stress on the correct syllable. Then use it in the target sentence.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen for the main stress in nominalisation and repeat the word before saying the sentence.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Nominalisation can create a more formal academic style.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˌnɒmɪnəlaɪˈzeɪʃən kən kriˈeɪt ə mɔː ˈfɔːməl ˌækəˈdemɪk staɪl/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place the main stress on the syllable 'za', in the ending -isation, and keep the remaining syllables clear.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the statement and the question aloud. Use falling intonation for the completed claim and rising intonation for the question.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Practise the difference between presenting a thesis and checking whether it is clear.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My thesis argues that public transport should be cheaper. Is the claim clear?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ ˈθiːsɪs ˈɑːɡjuːz ðət ˈpʌblɪk ˈtrænspɔːt ʃʊd bi ˈtʃiːpə | ɪz ðə kleɪm klɪə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Let your voice fall at the end of the thesis statement. Give the question a gentle rise to show that you are checking for understanding.
